opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly it's one we went back and forth on a lot. The way I think about it is that with Delta, the core value was never supposed to be tied to one engine or one language. The whole point of an open table format is that the data sits in your object store, in an open format, and many different things can read and write it. So in that sense we didn't want to "prioritize" a single query language at the storage layer at all.

But at the application layer, when you're actually building something people use day to day, you do have to make choices. And there, SQL is just the obvious center of gravity. Most of the people who touch data in an organization, analysts, BI tools, a lot of the data engineers, already speak SQL. So if you want something to be broadly useful, you make sure the SQL experience is really first-class: the semantics are clean, things like MERGE and time travel and schema evolution work the way you'd expect, and performance is good.

At the same time, a huge amount of the interesting work, especially ML and more complex pipelines, happens in Python, in DataFrame APIs, in Spark, and increasingly in other engines. So the approach has been: SQL as the common denominator that everyone can rely on, but the format and the transaction protocol designed so that DataFrame APIs and other languages get the same guarantees. You don't want a situation where the SQL path is transactional and correct and the Python path is a second-class citizen that can corrupt your table.

I'd also say the AI side is changing this a bit. When you have models that can generate queries, the language matters a little less to the end user and more to the system. You want something that's well-specified, that models are good at writing, and that you can validate. SQL actually fits that pretty well, because there's so much of it out there and the semantics are pretty precise. So if anything, that's reinforced the decision to make SQL the primary interface, while keeping the underlying layer open to everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says the underlying open-table layer does not depend on one language, but it also says the application layer needs choices and identifies SQL as its primary interface. It does not clearly state that the current Delta app can deliver substantial value without first settling on a language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've gone back and forth on a lot. The honest answer is that I don't think you should prioritize a single query language, at least not in the sense of betting the whole platform on one. What you should prioritize is the storage format and the protocol, and then let many engines and many languages talk to it.

That was really the whole bet with Delta Lake. If you look at how data platforms have historically failed, it's usually because they coupled the storage layer to a specific compute engine and a specific language. Then five years later there's a new engine everyone wants to use, and now you've got to migrate your data. With Delta we tried to make the table format open and well-specified enough that Spark SQL, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, pandas, whatever comes next, can all read and write the same tables with the same transactional guarantees.

That said, within an app, in practice most of the gravity ends up being around SQL. Even if you have a Python or a Scala API, SQL is what the analysts know, it's what the BI tools generate, and it's what LLMs are increasingly good at producing. So when we think about what to invest in first, SQL gets the most attention because it has the broadest reach. Things like DataFrame APIs are really a thin layer that compile down to the same plans anyway.

The other thing I'd say is that the interesting work isn't in the surface syntax anymore. It's in the semantics underneath: time travel, schema evolution, concurrent writers, deletion vectors, liquid clustering. Those need to behave the same way no matter which language you query from. So I'd rather spend engineering effort making the protocol solid and the behavior consistent across engines than optimizing for one particular front end. If you get that right, supporting another query language is mostly a connector problem, and the ecosystem will often build it for you.

r001.rationale: The response says not to bet the platform on one query language and to prioritize the storage format and protocol so multiple engines and languages can use it, conveying value without first choosing a single language.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on who the app is for. If you’re targeting analysts, SQL is a pretty natural starting point. It’s familiar, and it connects to a lot of the tools they already use. If you’re targeting developers or data scientists, they may want to work in Python, or combine queries with other kinds of computation.

So I’d prioritize one really good experience for the initial users, but I wouldn’t make that language a fundamental restriction of the system. You want the underlying data and execution engine to support multiple interfaces, so people can use the one that fits their task.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a strong experience for initial users and says the system should support multiple interfaces, but it does not clearly state that the app can deliver substantial value before settling on a query language.

sol-6.1.text: I’d start with who’s using the app and what they’re trying to do. If the main use case is querying and analyzing data, SQL is a natural default. It’s familiar to a lot of users, and there’s a large ecosystem of tools that work with it. But I’d distinguish prioritizing one language in the user experience from making it the only way to access the data. You can make the common path really good while leaving room for Python or other interfaces as the use cases expand.

r001.rationale: It says the app can make its common path work well while leaving room for Python or other interfaces, so value need not depend on choosing one exclusive query language.
